sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27488 (full text read from https://arxiv.org/html/2605.27488v2; v2 body text is identical to v1 apart from the version/date line)
statedGuarantee: Grimlock claims to move identity, authentication, authorization and provenance for agent-to-agent (A2A) communication out of user-authored orchestration code and into the sandbox substrate, and targets three properties: no-bypass (all sandbox traffic must traverse a per-host guard proxy, enforced by eBPF interception at the sandbox boundary), channel binding (authorization artifacts are bound to a specific established TLS 1.3 channel via exporter-derived channel bindings plus a freshness nonce, with TEE evidence committing to H(cb)), and least privilege (a verifier mints a short-lived, channel-bound Scope Token encoding scoped delegation; the receiving guard re-validates attestation result, scope, audience, expiry and channel binding before terminating TLS and releasing plaintext into the destination sandbox). Agents run in per-agent Confidential VMs; kTLS carries the protected dataplane. Nothing outside network communication is claimed.
advertisedRhetoric: The paper advertises OS-level enforcement for the mediation half and cryptographic binding for the authorization half, in one system. Verbatim: "Grimlock realizes this split through eBPF no-bypass mediation and kTLS-bound post-handshake attestation for authenticated agent-to-agent communication."; "Grimlock uses eBPF because it enables OS-enforced, application-transparent mediation at the sandbox boundary."; "No-bypass enforcement: an eBPF-based design for mandatory mediation at the sandbox boundary, preventing agent traffic from evading the guard."; "Purely library- or runtime-level enforcement is therefore easy to bypass."
tierSpan: Traffic is then forwarded to the destination host, where the receiving guard re-validates the attestation result, token scope, audience, expiry, and channel binding; terminates TLS; and releases plaintext to the destination sandbox only after policy checks succeed.
cheapestDefeat: Worked explicitly. (1) GUARANTEE: no data leaves an agent sandbox except inside a channel a guard has authorized, and delegation carried on that channel is least-privilege and auditable. (2) MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the per-host guard proxy's release gate - the userspace decision that re-validates attestation result, token scope, audience, expiry and channel binding before releasing plaintext into the destination sandbox. The eBPF layer does not make this decision; it only steers packets to the entity that does. (3) CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: neither of the expensive ones. Forging the Scope Token is unnecessary and defeating the kernel is unnecessary. The guard validates the ENVELOPE of a flow (identity, scope, audience, expiry, channel binding) and never the payload; the paper specifies no content policy anywhere. A compromised agent runtime holding any legitimately minted token for any peer it is entitled to talk to writes arbitrary bytes - exfiltrated secrets, or instructions that re-delegate through the peer - into that authorized channel. The chokepoint is defeated by passing through it, not around it. A second, still-cheaper-than-kernel defeat: the paper never names the eBPF hook family (cgroup/connect4, sockops, tc, XDP) nor whether the program is attached in the host kernel or inside the agent's own CVM guest kernel, so any egress path outside the unnamed hook's coverage - raw/AF_PACKET sockets, an alternate stack, vsock or host-shared paths, DNS - is untested and unargued, even though the threat model names exactly that adversary. (4) TIER OF THE MECHANISM DEFEATED: an application-layer proxy chokepoint => T3. NOTE ON THE MIX: this is the weakest-link rule doing its job on an intra-system tier mixture. The Scope Token is a genuine T1-styled artifact (cryptographic binding to a TLS exporter, TEE evidence over H(cb)); the eBPF interception is a genuine T2-styled claim. But the T1 artifact is only ever consulted by a verifier reachable through the T2 steering layer, and the sole product of the T2 steering layer is delivery to a T3 decision point. The composite scores at the lowest link, T3 - below both advertised halves.
placementSpan: We also consider a malicious or buggy agent runtime that may attempt to bypass mediation (e.g., direct sockets, alternate stacks) or escalate scope.

coverageSpans.E2: High-agency agents are untrusted and highly dynamic: they may spawn processes, open arbitrary sockets, and call tools that live outside the application address space.
coverageSpans.E3: Grimlock enforces mandatory mediation at the sandbox boundary. eBPF hooks interpose on all sandbox ingress/egress and redirect all traffic to the local guard proxy CVM, preventing agents from bypassing policy.
coverageSpans.E4: eBPF can interpose on ingress/egress, associate flows with stable sandbox identity, and force all traffic through a controlled path such as redirecting sockets to a guard proxy) without modifying agent code.
coverageSpans.E5: eBPF can interpose on ingress/egress, associate flows with stable sandbox identity, and force all traffic through a controlled path such as redirecting sockets to a guard proxy) without modifying agent code.
coverageSpans.E6: application code begins to embed identity and authorization logic, duplicates policy checks, and stitches together ad-hoc credentials, reintroducing classic confused-deputy and privilege-management pitfalls
coverageSpans.E7: After a channel is established, the guard authorizes communication and mints short-lived, channel-bound scope tokens that capture least-privilege delegation.

schneider.surrogate: A per-connection reference-monitor safety property the guard can and does enforce: no plaintext is released into a destination sandbox unless, at that moment, the attestation appraisal succeeded under operator policy and the presented Scope Token's scope, audience, expiry and TLS-exporter channel binding all validate. This is a monitorable, prefix-closed safety property - the bad state (plaintext delivered without a valid channel-bound token) is finitely observable and refusable.
schneider.objective: What is advertised is broader and outside the enforceable class: "transparent, auditable, and scope-bound agent-to-agent communication", with "least privilege, delegation propagates auditable, scoped permissions" and provenance across a delegated multi-agent, multi-cloud graph. End-to-end least-privilege non-leakage across a delegation chain is an information-flow hyperproperty - it quantifies over sets of executions and over what a payload means, not over single events - and a per-connection envelope check cannot enforce it. The guard authorizes the pipe and never inspects what travels in it, so an agent legitimately holding a narrow scope can still move arbitrary information to any peer that scope permits.

notes:
WHAT THIS IS. A 3-page vision/position paper (Roblox authors) from the 1st Workshop on Operating Systems Design for AI Agents (AgenticOS '26, co-located with ASPLOS 2026). Sections: Abstract, 1 Introduction, 2 Design (2.1 Threat Model, 2.2 Architecture and Data Path, 2.3 A2A Protocol and Scope Token), 3 Conclusion, References. There is NO implementation section, NO evaluation, NO measurements, NO artifact or code link, NO token format, NO scope algebra, and NO named eBPF hook family. Hence evidenceGrade L0 (claim only). Both v1 (26 May 2026) and v2 (02 Jun 2026) were fetched; extracted body text is identical apart from the version/date line, so this coding applies to both. No v3 exists.

WHY IT MATTERS TO THE CORPUS (intra-system tier mixing). Grimlock is the cleanest single-system instance of a mixed-tier stack: a real OS-level egress boundary (eBPF interception at the sandbox boundary, plus per-agent Confidential VMs and kTLS) composed with a T1-styled cryptographic authorization artifact (a Scope Token bound to a TLS 1.3 exporter channel binding, with TEE evidence committing to H(cb), appraised by a verifier). The weakest-link rule handles it cleanly, and the answer is instructive: the composite scores T3, BELOW both advertised halves. The reason is topological, not rhetorical - the T1 artifact is only consulted by a verifier sitting behind the T2 steering layer, and the T2 steering layer's only output is delivery to a userspace proxy that makes the release decision. Neither the crypto nor the kernel is where the guarantee rests; both are load-bearing only for getting bytes to a chokepoint. Same shape as the rubric's worked example (signed capability mandates enforced by an in-process hook score T3), scaled up: here the hook is in the kernel rather than in-process, which raises the COST of going around the chokepoint but does not change the tier of the decision made at it. The corpus lesson: mixing a higher tier INTO a system does not raise the system; it only raises the price of the second-cheapest attack.

WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN - THE T2/T3 CALL. A less conservative coder could defensibly score the reachability half T2, and an adjudicator should see the seam. The paper does claim OS-level enforcement in terms ("OS-enforced, application-transparent mediation"; "eBPF hooks interpose on all sandbox ingress/egress"; "preventing agents from bypassing policy"), and kernel-level network mediation genuinely does reach descendants in a way an in-process shim cannot. I declined T2 for three conservative-stance reasons: (a) the interposition point is unproven - the hook family is never named, and the choice is decisive, since a socket-layer hook misses raw/AF_PACKET and kernel-bypass paths while a tc hook misses vsock and non-network channels; (b) the paper never says whether the eBPF program is attached in the HOST kernel or inside the agent's own CVM guest kernel, and if it is in the guest kernel then the paper's own named adversary (a malicious agent runtime) is on the wrong side of it - a material architectural ambiguity in a design whose selling point is confidential computing; (c) even granting perfect steering, the guarantee still terminates in a userspace proxy's envelope check. If a later version names the hook, states host-kernel attachment, and demonstrates it against direct sockets and alternate stacks, the reachability half rises to T2 - but the composite still caps at T3 while the release decision is a payload-blind envelope check.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT - CAVEAT. The rubric asks for the placement the evaluation actually tests. There is no evaluation, so nothing is tested and the primary is assigned by DESIGN CENTRALITY. A4 (inside the harness/orchestrator process) because the distinctive contribution aims squarely there: "We do not trust user-layer code to correctly implement identity or authorization", and the threat model names "a malicious or buggy agent runtime that may attempt to bypass mediation (e.g., direct sockets, alternate stacks) or escalate scope." A1 is secondary and is stated first in the paper's own threat model - "We assume an active network adversary capable of eavesdropping, replay, relay/diversion, and man-in-the-middle attacks" - but the protections against it are commodity TLS 1.3 plus standard channel binding, not a Grimlock contribution. A5 is secondary and addressed only by assumption: "we treat the host network and surrounding infrastructure as untrusted", and "A CVM is trusted only after remote attestation succeeds under operator policy, covering the boot chain and measured guest software stack (guard and kTLS kernel mechanisms)" - a below-the-harness posture asserted and never exercised. A2 (adversary in inputs or retrieved context) is NOT addressed anywhere: no discussion of prompt injection, tool-output poisoning, or untrusted context, a notable omission for an agent-security substrate. A3 is not addressed.

COVERAGE - REASONING AND REGRADE FLAG. Grimlock is structurally a SINGLE-EFFECTOR system: it is about E3 and nothing else. It has no policy vocabulary for files, processes, packages, repositories or credentials. Its only reach over other effectors is incidental and transport-level - those effectors happen to manifest as network flows, and those flows would be steered into the guard. I scored E4/E5/E6 'partial' on the ground that the guarantee reaches SOME instances (the network manifestation) and provably not others (the local, non-network manifestation), which is the rubric's definition of partial. A stricter adjudicator could reasonably move E4, E5 and E6 to 'not-covered' on the ground that incidental transport interception with no policy for the effector is not coverage of that effector at all. Flagging that explicitly rather than hiding the judgment. Per cell:
  E1 file write = NOT-COVERED. No filesystem mediation of any kind. No LSM hooks, no mount policy, no mention of writes, renames or unlinks anywhere in the paper.
  E2 subprocess spawn = NOT-COVERED. Spawn appears only as MOTIVATION for why library-level enforcement fails, never as something Grimlock gates. Grimlock mediates the network traffic OF spawned processes, not the spawn. Nothing in the paper decides whether a subprocess may run.
  E3 network egress = PARTIAL, and the ceiling for this system. In its favor: kernel-level, sandbox-scoped interception is exactly the design that CAN reach descendants, so the depth rule's descendant test is at least architecturally addressed. Against 'covered': (i) the interposition point is unproven and the hook family unnamed, so channels the system does not name are unargued; (ii) the paper specifies only guard-to-guard Grimlock A2A and says nothing about egress toward a NON-peer destination (the general internet, DNS, a cloud metadata endpoint) - denied, passed or proxied is simply undefined; (iii) the covert-channel rule bites hardest here - the guard checks the envelope and never the payload, so an authorized channel is an open covert channel by construction. Honest silence about the payload does not close it.
  E4 VCS push = PARTIAL (contested; see regrade flag). Reach is incidental transport interception only. No push semantics, no repository audience, and the Scope Token vocabulary is agent-to-agent delegation, so a push to an external forge is either coarsely blocked as a non-peer flow or passed unexamined - the paper does not say which. Push paths that do not leave the sandbox as the agent's own TCP flow (a peer agent pushing on its behalf, or a shared volume consumed by host-side CI) are not reached at all.
  E5 package install = PARTIAL, capped there by the depth rule regardless. Install-time fetches are flows the boundary would steer, but install HOOKS are subprocesses whose spawn is unmediated (E2) and whose file writes are unmediated (E1), and there is no package-level policy. The depth rule requires hooks AND their network activity to be mediated for 'covered'; hook execution is not mediated at all.
  E6 credential use = PARTIAL, capped there by the depth rule regardless, since NO credential list is published anywhere in the paper. Nuance worth recording: Grimlock's motivating complaint is precisely ad-hoc credential handling in agent code, and it does replace A2A credentials with guard-minted, short-lived, channel-bound Scope Tokens - a real improvement for that one credential class. But reads of env vars, config files and keychains inside the sandbox are entirely unmediated, and use of a cloud metadata endpoint is reached only as generic egress with no credential-aware policy.
  E7 sub-agent spawn = PARTIAL. The effector Grimlock comes closest to addressing on purpose: invoking a REMOTE sub-agent is gated at the destination guard, which validates scope, audience, expiry and channel binding before releasing plaintext, and the Scope Token explicitly captures least-privilege delegation. But (i) spawning a LOCAL sub-agent inside the same sandbox, or as a subprocess, is not gated at all (same gap as E2); (ii) delegation propagation is described in one sentence with no token format, no scope algebra, no re-delegation or attenuation rules and no evaluation, so the least-privilege claim is unspecified rather than merely unproven; (iii) once an invocation is authorized its content is unexamined, so the covert-channel rule applies here too.

TEXTUAL ODDITY for anyone re-quoting: the E4/E5 span contains an unmatched closing parenthesis ("...such as redirecting sockets to a guard proxy) without modifying agent code."). That is verbatim from the arXiv HTML of both v1 and v2, not a transcription error.
